source.title: Variational operator learning: A unified paradigm marrying training neural operators and solving partial differential equations
source.authors: Tengfei Xu; Dachuan Liu; Peng Hao; Bo Wang

record.tranche_reason: Extends power-law-style scaling to PDE solution-operator learning, reporting test error against the amount of unlabeled training data.
record.gate_note: The paper's own scaling experiment varies training-data size and reports test-error curves. It does not test language-model loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute, or predict larger language-model runs. The cited language-model scaling works are context, not results from this study. Worst-case test errors are described as decreasing with training-set size but are not reported as power-law fits.
record.test_reason: The study varies the amount of unlabeled training data for FNO-based neural operators on four PDE benchmarks. It fits test error to y = ax^b and reports polynomial convergence in all cases. That is a data-scaling power-law result in a non-language setting, so it bears on V5 only. Language-model claims V1–V4, V6 and V7 are cited as context, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say VOL test errors follow a power law in the amount of unlabeled data, explicitly 'like LLMs' (citing Kaplan et al.), and that VOL learns solution operators well given enough cheap unlabeled data.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains FNO-based PDE solution operators and measures test error against training-data size; it does not use the language-model scaling-law measurement or variables.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports the scaling experiment across four different PDE benchmarks. It does not report a comparison of fitted scaling exponents or fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Worst-case test error falls as the training set grows on all four benchmarks. At N=10000 the worst-case errors are 6.64%, 11.69%, 3.33% and 7.14%. No power-law fit is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In PDE operator learning, worst-case test error decreases with more unlabeled training data.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of the mechanics and physics of solids
record.problems: The scaling curves and coefficients are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text; the reported measure is PDE test error rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss, and only training-data amount is varied.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling rows omitted. Other reported experiments, including resolution and optimization-strategy comparisons, do not measure the power-law scaling behavior covered by the tested version.

untested.parts: Only test error against unlabeled training-set size is tested, with no variation in model size or compute. The range of data sizes (only the maximum, 10000, is stated), the number of orders of magnitude covered, and the fitted exponents are not recoverable from the text. Other modalities and regimes are not tested.

missing.what: Range of training-set sizes used in the scaling experiment, and the fitted coefficients a and b per benchmark. The text says the coefficients are in Fig. 2a, but the extracted text is truncated here.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak T3 test of V5. The scaling axis is data only, the evidence is figure-only, and the extent of the range is unknown. The paper's other experiments (resolution, generalization benefits, optimization strategies) do not bear on any version. The source text around the scaling-experiment description is garbled or truncated.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between language-model parameters and tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.

Only test error versus unlabeled training-data amount in the reported PDE benchmarks is tested; other modalities and training regimes, and scaling against language-model parameters, tokens, or compute, are not tested.
Downstream task performance and its relationship to language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and whether language-model curves bend away from a power law.
